newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope gives thanks for year, looks to millenium.
newsitem.headline: Pope gives thanks for year, looks to millenium.

text.p: Pope John Paul, looking back at the past year and ahead to the approaching millenium, officiated at the traditional "Te Deum" vespers in the Jesuit church of St Ignatius Loyola in central Rome on Tuesday.
The 76-year-old Polish Pope, addressing the faithful at the end of a year in which he underwent an appendix operation in October, gave thanks for what had been achieved.

"This evening, in this magnificent church in the centre of the city, in our giving of thanks we would like to mention every good deed of God carried out by the apostolic ministry both in the universal Church and in our city," he said.

"I would like to thank the Lord, in a special way, for the results achieved during the year that is ending, during which, as the end of the second millenium nears, we have begun preparations for the Great Jubilee," he added.

The Pope has declared the year 2000 to be a Catholic Holy Year and he hoped, in remarks directed at the civil authorities present, that there would be no "lack of commitment" by all to help transform the city for the Jubilee.
Last December, the Pope called on the faithful to give money to a campaign to help build more churches in Rome for the year 2000 and show the city had a "Christian heart".
The Italian capital already has nearly 1,000 Catholic churches, including St Peter's Basilica.
The start of the third millennium is expected to attract perhaps history's biggest pilgrimages to Rome. The 50 new churches that the Pope wants built will be in the outskirts.
The Pope, who skipped Christmas Day mass in St Peter's Basilica on medical advice, looked in relatively good form as he read the homily, sitting down as is customary.
